clue.text: Not quite twelve — sleep lightly

indicators.note: not quite means the word for twelve stops one letter short of its end

parts.note: twelve is a dozen

explanation.surface: Someone nods off just before midnight, never sleeping deeply.
explanation.definitionFit: To nod off briefly or snooze is to sleep lightly.

clue.text: Last, nevertheless

definitions.meaning: in the sense 'in the end, finally', as in 'he came last of all'
in the sense 'in spite of that, however'

explanation.surface: Two terse words that read like a fragment of argument.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means both 'finally, in the end' and 'despite everything, however'.

clue.text: Left section with editor

parts.note: a section is a part

explanation.surface: A newspaper section that left with its editor, as if staff walked out.
explanation.definitionFit: Left as a past verb means departed or went away, the same as separated company.

clue.text: Barge in on a brat, upset about argument

indicators.note: about means those rearranged letters go around the word for argument
upset means the letters of 'on a brat' are knocked over into a new order

parts.note: a row is a quarrel or argument

explanation.surface: Someone barges in on a spoilt child who is upset about a quarrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barge in' reads as a phrasal verb, but 'Barge' alone is the noun definition and 'in' is a link. 'upset' turns ON A BRAT into NARBOAT; 'about' wraps that round ROW.
explanation.definitionFit: A long, slim canal boat is a kind of barge, a flat-bottomed vessel for inland waterways.

clue.text: Available for one wrongly parted by force

indicators.note: parted by means the rearranged letters are split open with another letter inside
wrongly means the letters of 'for one' are put in the wrong order

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for force in physics

explanation.surface: Something available to one person, wrongly separated from them by force.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrongly' turns FOR ONE into ONOFER, which is 'parted by' F placed in its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Goods that are for sale or obtainable are said to be available.

clue.text: Perhaps Wilde's opening scene caused another rumpus initially

parts.note: an opening or hole is shaped like the letter O

indicators.note: initially means take the first letter of each of the four words before it

explanation.surface: The first night of a Wilde play, whose opening scene sparked another row.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wilde's opening' looks like W, but 's is a link ('has'), and 'opening' gives O. Oscar Wilde is the Irish playwright; 'Perhaps' marks him as one example of the name.
explanation.definitionFit: Oscar was the first name of the writer Wilde, so Wilde is one instance of someone so named.

clue.text: Heavy wave sweeping over vessel in fairground ride

indicators.note: in a down clue, sweeping over means the first piece sits above the second

parts.note: a roller is a long heavy wave breaking on the shore
a coaster is a ship that trades along the coast

explanation.surface: A huge wave crashes over a ship in the middle of a funfair ride.
explanation.definitionFit: A switchback railway with steep drops and loops is a classic amusement park thrill.

clue.text: A complex network to take one's breath away

parts.note: a maze is a complex network of paths

explanation.surface: A tangled system so intricate it leaves you breathless.
explanation.definitionFit: To astonish or stun someone is to leave them breathless with wonder.

clue.text: Form of English inlet

definitions.meaning: ... English is a south-eastern British accent spreading out from London along the Thames
a tidal mouth of a river where it meets the sea

explanation.surface: A dictionary-style note on a type of English and a coastal inlet.
explanation.walkthrough: Estuary English is the name for a London-influenced accent of south-east England, named after the Thames estuary.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a tidal river mouth and, by extension, a regional British accent.

clue.text: Beginning to scare me, describing revolutionary's plot

indicators.note: describing in the sense of drawing a line round means the outer letters enclose another piece
beginning to means take only the first letter of the word scare

parts.note: Che Guevara is the archetypal revolutionary

explanation.surface: Someone is frightened by a revolutionary's conspiracy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'describing' is used in its geometric sense of drawing a line round something, so it signals containment.
explanation.definitionFit: A plot is a secret plan or conspiracy, a crafty design.

clue.text: Learned line to repeat

parts.note: to iterate is to repeat

explanation.surface: An actor having learned a line and now running it again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Learned' looks like a past tense verb, but it is the adjective meaning educated.
explanation.definitionFit: A well-read, educated person who can read and write well is learned.

clue.text: Squash up, then continue

parts.note: to squash is to press
up as in a game score means ahead, in the lead

explanation.surface: Instructions for packing: squeeze things in tight, then carry on.
explanation.definitionFit: To carry on determinedly despite obstacles is to proceed or keep going.

clue.text: No doubt convinced, stop it!

parts.note: to be convinced is to be sure
the exclamation 'Enough!' tells someone to stop

explanation.surface: An exasperated person, certain of something, telling another to give it a rest.
explanation.definitionFit: An adverb phrase meaning certainly or indeed, as expected.

clue.text: Rebuke after wife stole

indicators.note: after means the rebuke follows the letter for wife

parts.note: a rap is a sharp rebuke, as in a rap over the knuckles

explanation.surface: A husband tells off his wife after she has stolen something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stole' looks like a past tense verb but is the noun: a scarf or shawl.
explanation.definitionFit: A stole is a shawl worn round the shoulders, something you drape around yourself.

clue.text: Tale of woe, as difficult chance goes to waste around close of play

parts.note: difficult means hard
chance means luck

indicators.note: around here means turned back to front, the decaying word read backwards

parts.note: something that goes to waste rots

indicators.note: close of means the last letter of the word play

explanation.surface: A sad story of a hard game where a lucky chance was squandered at the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' looks like a containment signal before 'close of play', but here it turns the rotting word back to front.
explanation.definitionFit: An account of misfortune told to win sympathy is a sorrowful narrative.

clue.text: Raleigh, at sea, produces something for shock?

indicators.note: at sea means confused, so the letters of Raleigh are jumbled

explanation.surface: Sir Walter Raleigh on a voyage produces something to cause a shock.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'shock' of hair is a thick mass of it; the question mark flags this pun.
explanation.definitionFit: A styling product holds a thick mop of hair in place.

clue.text: Piece of pork over — starts to reheat it on top of barbecue

parts.note: over in the sense of left over means spare

indicators.note: starts to means take the first letters of reheat and it
in a down clue, top of means the first letter of barbecue

explanation.surface: Leftover pork to be warmed up on the barbecue.
explanation.definitionFit: A cut of pork ribs with most of the meat trimmed off is a familiar barbecue dish.

clue.text: Some up in eucalyptus tree

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A koala, perhaps, somewhere high up in a gum tree.
explanation.definitionFit: A conifer with needles and cones is a common evergreen.

clue.text: Corrupt deal, by implication?

indicators.note: by implication says the clue word is what the answer implies when read as an instruction, not what builds it

parts.note: read as instructions, the answer sends the four-letter word for guide wrong, and those letters rearranged make deal

explanation.surface: A corrupt deal, implied rather than stated outright.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: 'by implication' says the answer, read as wordplay with 'astray' as an anagram signal, implies the clue word.
explanation.definitionFit: To corrupt someone is to tempt them into wrongdoing, steering them off the right path.

clue.text: Allowed to keep article over in outhouse

indicators.note: to keep means the word for allowed holds the article inside it

parts.note: allowed means let
an is the indefinite article
O is the cricket scorebook abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: Someone permitted to store an item over in a shed.
explanation.definitionFit: A simple shed built against a wall is a kind of small outbuilding.

clue.text: Serious crime of beheaded parish priest

indicators.note: beheaded means the first letter is cut off

parts.note: a parson is a parish priest

explanation.surface: A grim tale of a vicar who had his head cut off.
explanation.definitionFit: Deliberately setting fire to property is a grave criminal offence.

clue.text: Rating on manoeuvres in the dark

indicators.note: manoeuvres means the letters are moved about into a new order

explanation.surface: A naval rating out on night exercises.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on manoeuvres' reads as one phrase, but 'on' is part of the letters to rearrange, with 'manoeuvres' alone signalling the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in the dark about something is to be unaware or uninformed.

clue.text: Undergraduate ultimately failing to pass

indicators.note: ultimately means take the final letter of undergraduate

parts.note: a failing or slip is a lapse

explanation.surface: A student who ends up failing to get through the exam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pass' suggests an exam, but here it is the verb used of time.
explanation.definitionFit: Time going by is said to pass or slip away.

clue.text: Charitable donations to the needy members, we hear

indicators.note: we hear means the word sounds like another when spoken

parts.note: arms are limbs, which are bodily members

explanation.surface: Members of a club giving to the poor, so we are told.
explanation.walkthrough: In a non-rhotic British accent the word for limbs sounds the same as this one.
explanation.definitionFit: Money or food given to the poor as charity, an old-fashioned term.

clue.text: Unimportant match

explanation.surface: A trivial sporting fixture.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both trivial, of little weight, and a flame for a cigarette.

clue.text: Film of artist popular with staff

parts.note: RA is a Royal Academician, an artist
in means popular or fashionable
to staff is to man

explanation.surface: An artist who gets on well with the workers.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1988 movie starring Dustin Hoffman and Tom Cruise is a well-known picture.
